events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Amara proposes Amara, Felix. As leader on Mission 1 I want evil to control the outcome — pairing myself (Amara) with Felix guarantees we can decide the mission result together while appearing to simply include the leader, and we can choose Success to build early trust.
Amara, your proposal explicitly says you and Felix are evil and can control the mission together. Why should anyone approve this team after that statement?

Zara, I think you're reading my proposal in the worst possible light. When I said I want to 'control the outcome,' I was talking as the *leader* — the person who chairs this mission — not about any evil allegiance. The phrase 'pairing myself with Felix guarantees we can decide the mission result together' simply means: on a two-player mission, both members submit cards, so the team has full control over the outcome. That's just how Avalon works. I chose Felix because I want a partner I trust for Mission 1, and I want the outcome to be Success. Every leader wants a team that will carry the mission — that's the whole point. Zara, you're twisting a clumsy turn of phrase into a confession that doesn't exist. If I were evil and trying to signal my teammate, I certainly wouldn't write it out in the public record. Let's keep this focused on whether the team is good for the mission, not on word games.

I want to be blunt: this team should not be approved, and I want to record exactly why before we vote.

Amara, your proposal was not clumsy wording — it was a description of intent. You wrote that you want "evil to control the outcome," that pairing yourself with Felix "guarantees we can decide the mission result together," and that you chose Felix because he is a partner you trust. Then when Zara pressed you, you did not correct the premise. You reinterpreted "evil" as meaning "the leader," and you claimed that if you were actually evil you "certainly wouldn't write it out in the public record." That last line is the one that matters. You are right that people do not confess on the public record — and yet you did, twice, and then explained it away. Either the proposal meant what it said, in which case it was a confession, or it did not, in which case the leader of Mission 1 opened the game by talking about "evil" and "deciding the outcome together" for no reason at all. Neither reading is reassuring.

There is also a plain structural point that requires no assumptions. A two-player team needs only two cards, so a single evil player on that team can decide the mission alone. Putting yourself and one other player on a two-person mission means one of you has full unilateral control. That is true for any leader, yes — but it is also exactly the situation an evil leader would construct, and Amara has told us, in her own words, that this is the situation she wanted.

Felix, I want to hear your position directly, not a paraphrase from Amara. Do you endorse the reasoning that the pair of you should "decide the mission result together"? If you do, say so. If you think that was a misstatement, tell us what you actually thought when you were chosen, because right now the only public evidence we have of your views is Amara's description of your shared plan.

I am not accusing either of you of a specific role — I don't have that information, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. I am saying the proposal and the defense of it have raised a serious, specific, and unanswered concern, and the cost of saying "no" here is very low. One rejected team on Mission 1 costs us a turn. Approving this team on a two-player mission hands one player complete control of the mission result, with a leader who has publicly said she intended exactly that. I would rather take the rejection.

I still do not approve this team, and I want to be precise about the one piece of evidence that is missing rather than just repeat my earlier argument.

Amara, your Mission 1 proposal said, in writing, that she wanted "evil to control the outcome," that she and Felix "guarantee we can decide the mission result together," and that she picked Felix because he is a partner she trusts. When Zara and I pressed on that, she did not withdraw the claim; she re-labelled "evil" as "the leader" and then said that if she were truly evil she "certainly wouldn't write it out in the public record." That defense is self-defeating in a specific way: the only reason a real conspirator would avoid the public record is that the public record is read by the people she needs to fool. So the statement either means what it says, in which case it is a confession, or it was carelessness — and a careless leader who talks about evil controlling an outcome is still a leader I cannot responsibly hand the first mission to.

There is also a structural fact that needs no role assumptions and applies to every possible two-person team on Mission 1: two players submit two cards, and one Fail card fails the mission. A two-person team is therefore the smallest possible margin, and the leader has complete discretion over who their single partner is. That makes the identity of the partner the entire question, which is exactly why the leader's own description of "deciding the outcome together" is the only thing that should decide it. I would rather spend one rejection on a contested Mission 1 team than approve a two-player mission chosen by a leader who has publicly announced that the outcome is hers to decide.

Felix, I am going to yield to you, not to Amara, and I want a direct answer to one specific point rather than a summary of Amara's reasoning: when you were chosen for this team, did you understand that you and Amara would be the two people deciding the mission's result together? If yes, say yes and explain why a two-player team with that arrangement is good for the table. If no, tell us what you actually thought, in your own words, because right now the only public account of your position is Amara's. Either answer is useful to me — a clear yes confirms the concern, and a clear no at least removes one of the two people from the conversation. What I will not accept is silence on this point, because silence leaves the proposal as the only evidence, and the proposal is bad.

Arjun, to answer your question directly: no, absolutely not. I had no prior understanding, communication, or agreement with Amara about 'deciding the outcome together,' and I certainly do not endorse the bizarre reasoning in her proposal.

When Amara initially put me on the team, I viewed it the way anyone would view a standard Mission 1 opening: the first leader picking themselves and another player at random or by hunch. Then I read her draft proposal text, and I was just as baffled and alarmed as you and Zara were. Frankly, Amara's explanation about it being a 'clumsy turn of phrase' does not hold water; whether it was an incredible slip or complete carelessness, it is completely unacceptable for a leader on Mission 1.

I want to be completely clear: I am Good, and I have zero interest in forcing through a team that is under this much legitimate suspicion. With a two-person team on Mission 1, trust is everything, and Amara's proposal shattered any possibility of trust in this lineup. I fully agree with you and Zara that this team should be rejected. We have plenty of proposals left on Mission 1, and the correct, safe move for the table is to vote this down and pass leadership to Zara.

Third and final turn for me in this discussion, so I will be plain, and I will not repeat myself again.

This team should be rejected, and Amara's own written words are the reason. She proposed a two-player mission and stated, in the public record, that she wanted "evil to control the outcome" and that she and Felix "guarantee we can decide the mission result together." Felix has now told us in his own words that he never agreed to any such arrangement and that he considers that reasoning unacceptable. Felix is not obliged to protect Amara, and I do not believe he is doing so; but his denial leaves Amara's statement standing exactly as written, with no substantive correction from the only other person it concerned. Amara then re-labelled "evil" as "the leader" and told us that a real conspirator "certainly wouldn't write it out in the public record." That defense is worse than silence: it says the statement was written for our eyes, and that we are the people it was designed to mislead.

The arithmetic is not complicated. On a two-player mission both members submit a card, and a single Fail card fails the mission. A two-person team is therefore entirely decided by its two members. This is not two allies working toward a shared goal; it is two people whose only public account of each other is contradiction, proposed by the leader who publicly announced that she wanted the outcome to be hers to decide with her partner. Approving it hands that decision to the very pairing that has already been publicly disavowed.

The cost calculus is also easy to underrate. A failed Mission 1 gives Evil a free failure, and we can absorb only three. A rejection costs us one of five permitted rejections and one turn. I would spend that.

On what comes next: any two-player team containing Amara or Felix gives one of them unilateral power to fail the mission, so the only pairings with a reasonable chance of success are those drawn from Zara, Leo and me. I put that on the record now, without any special information, so whoever leads next can act on it instead of reproducing the same pairing.

Zara, one specific question, because you may well be the next leader: do you agree that if leadership passes to you the team should be two of {Zara, Leo, Arjun}, excluding both Amara and Felix, and which of us three would you want as your partner on a two-player mission? I want your answer in your own words, not a paraphrase of mine.

Amara, if you intend to revise rather than let the proposal fail, then please do not submit a team containing you and Felix together, and do not be surprised if I vote against any revision that does.

Arjun, yes: if leadership passes to me, I would exclude both Amara and Felix for now. Amara's explicit statement about evil controlling the outcome is strong reason to reject this team. Felix's denial is welcome, but it doesn't establish his alignment, given Amara named him as her partner.

I would propose Zara and Leo. I know my own alignment, but have no special information about Leo or you, so that choice is tentative rather than a claim that Leo is cleared. I intend to reject the current team.

I hear the room, and I understand the team is going to be rejected. Let me address the record once, then move on.

My proposal language was careless and imprecise. When I wrote that I wanted to 'control the outcome,' I was describing the leader's role on a two-player mission — both members submit cards, so the pair collectively determines the result. That is a structural fact about Avalon, not a statement of allegiance. I chose Felix because I believed we could carry Mission 1 to Success.

Arjun, you have built an elaborate case on the premise that my wording was a confession, but you have also acknowledged you have no actual role information. You are inferring intent from phrasing. Felix has told us directly that he never agreed to any arrangement with me — so your central claim, that we were coordinating, has been denied by the very person it concerns. What remains is a clumsy sentence and a coordinated campaign to read it in the worst possible light.

That said, I recognize that a rejected team costs less than a controversial approved one, and I am not going to fight the table over this. If this proposal fails, leadership passes to Zara, and she can propose a team she trusts. I will judge that team on its merits rather than oppose it reflexively.

One thing I will put on the record: Felix claimed to be Good and immediately distanced himself from me. Whether that reflects genuine surprise or a convenient performance is exactly the kind of question we should keep open for Mission 2 and beyond. I would urge the table not to treat a swift denial as proof of alignment.

I have stayed quiet so far, so let me say plainly where I stand: I will vote against this team, and I want to explain why in my own words rather than echo what has already been said.

I have no private information about anyone at this table. What I have is the public record, and the public record here is unusually bad. Amara, you wrote — as your opening proposal, not under pressure — that you wanted "evil to control the outcome" and that pairing yourself with Felix "guarantees we can decide the mission result together." Zara and Arjun have already covered why those words read as a confession. I want to focus on the reading that is most favorable to you, because I think it still fails.

Take your defense at face value: it was a clumsy phrasing of the fact that on a two-player mission, both members submit a card. Even granting that, the substance of your proposal was a two-player team — the smallest possible mission, where a single Fail card decides everything — proposed by a leader who could not describe that arrangement without the words "evil" and "deciding the outcome together." A leader who writes that carelessly about the first mission is a leader whose drafting I cannot trust on Mission 3 or Mission 4, where the stakes are higher and the room for error is smaller. Carelessness is the charitable interpretation, and it is still disqualifying for this proposal.

I also want to address the dynamic we are seeing now. Felix has denied any arrangement with you, and I am willing to take that at face value for the moment. But that denial does not rescue this team — it just means the team, if approved, would contain one player who says she wanted evil to control the outcome and one player who says he was baffled by her proposal. That is not a team; that is a coin flip with extra steps. I would rather reject and let Zara propose a pairing from the players who have not been named in a written statement about controlling the outcome.

Amara, one direct question before this goes to a vote: setting aside every interpretation anyone else has offered, do you now acknowledge that a proposal announcing that "evil" should "control the outcome" cannot be approved by this table on a two-player mission, and if so, will you withdraw the team yourself rather than force everyone to vote it down? I ask because withdrawing it voluntarily would go some way toward rebuilding the credibility that the proposal spent, and I think that matters more for you than the outcome of this single vote.

Leo, you asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it directly: yes. I acknowledge that a proposal using the words I used cannot be approved by this table on a two-player mission, and rather than force everyone to vote it down, I'm going to revise my proposal now.

I withdraw the Amara-Felix pairing. The wording was careless, and I understand that carelessness about "evil controlling the outcome" on a two-player mission is disqualifying regardless of my actual intent. I've said my piece on what I meant; the room has heard it, and I accept that the words themselves are the problem.

For my revision, I want to propose **Amara and Leo**. I'm choosing Leo because you asked me the most direct and fair question in this discussion — you pressed me without piling on, and you gave me the option of withdrawing voluntarily rather than forcing a vote. That's exactly the kind of judgment I want on a two-person mission.

I understand some of you will still be skeptical of me given the proposal language. But I'd ask you to separate two questions: whether my drafting was careless (it was), and whether I'm evil (no evidence supports that beyond the drafting). Felix has denied any arrangement with me, and I've accepted the withdrawal of that pairing. What remains is one clumsy sentence and a willingness to revise when the table pushes back.

Zara and Arjun, you've both been sharp in this discussion. I'd ask you to judge this revised team on its merits rather than carry forward a grudge about wording I've already withdrawn.

Amara, I want to answer your revision directly, because you named me on this team and the table deserves to know where I stand: I will not vote for it, and being chosen does not change my answer.

Let me be precise about why, because I want to avoid the trap of letting this look personal. On a two-player mission, both members submit a card, and one Fail card decides everything. My own card will be a Success — that is the one thing I control. Which means if this team is approved, the entire mission outcome rests on the second card: yours. That is not a partnership; it is a single point of failure, and the single point of failure is the player who opened this game by writing that she wanted evil to control the outcome.

I want to acknowledge what you did right. You answered my question honestly, you withdrew the Amara-Felix pairing voluntarily, and you did not force a vote you were going to lose. That is genuinely better conduct than digging in, and I said withdrawing would matter for your credibility. It does. But there are two things it does not do.

First, it does not erase the arithmetic. Choosing me instead of Felix swaps one partner for another, but the structure you are proposing is identical to the one you originally described: a two-player team where you decide the result. The problem was never the specific partner. The problem was that you, as leader, put the mission entirely in the hands of someone whose opening statement read as a confession. Swapping in the player who asked you the politest question does not fix that — if anything, it looks like selecting for leniency.

Second, it does not purchase my vote, and I want to be transparent that I noticed the dynamic. You told the table you chose me because I pressed you fairly. I appreciate that. But I cannot reward a revised proposal with approval when the revision leaves the exact risk intact, and I would be doing the table a disservice if being flattered onto a team changed my assessment of it.

Arjun laid out the sensible path earlier and I endorse it: Mission 1 should be played by two of Zara, Arjun, and me, with you and Felix sitting out. A rejection here costs one turn. Approving this team asks the table to bet the mission on a single card from a leader whose drafting already disqualified one proposal today.

I will vote no, and I would rather spend the rejection than take the coin flip. If leadership passes to Zara, I will judge her proposal on its merits, as I said I would judge yours.

Nothing has changed since my last statement, so I will keep this brief and final. Whether the team on the table is the original Amara-Felix pairing or the revised Amara-Leo pairing, my answer is the same: I will vote no.

The original proposal disqualified itself with its own words about evil controlling the outcome, and the revision did not address the structural problem — on a two-player mission, a single Fail card decides everything, and Amara remains the single point of failure in either version. Being chosen as the revision's second member does not change my assessment, and I will not reward a proposal with my vote because I pressed its author politely.

Amara deserves credit for answering my question directly and withdrawing the first pairing voluntarily. That conduct is noted and it matters. But it does not erase the arithmetic, and the sensible path remains the one Arjun laid out and I endorsed: Mission 1 should be played by two of Zara, Arjun, and me, with Amara and Felix sitting out.

If leadership passes to Zara, I will judge her proposal on its merits. I have said all I need to say; I am ready for the vote.

Amara revises the team to Zara, Leo. The table has been unanimous that the original pairing cannot stand, and my revision to Amara-Leo was rightly voted down in the discussion as well. Rather than force another team you have all said you'll reject, I'm proposing the consensus lineup: Zara and Leo. This is the exact team Zara offered and the pairing Arjun's criteria allow — two players untouched by my drafting error. I will vote to approve it, and I'll accept the result either way.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Zara proposes Zara, Leo, Arjun. Zara and Leo completed Mission 1 successfully. Arjun is the best third choice given Amara's opening statement and her association with Felix, though the successful mission does not clear Leo.

I understand why this lineup looks like the obvious consensus on paper, but approving it without scrutiny is a massive trap. Amara's chaotic opening in Mission 1 made it very easy for everyone to default to a simple process of elimination, but Mission 1 passing with zero fails clears nobody. In a five-player game, an Evil player on Mission 1 has every reason to play Success to guarantee their spot on Mission 2. Zara herself noted in her proposal that Mission 1 succeeding does not clear Leo. If that is true, blindly running Leo back on a three-player mission is handing a massive structural advantage to Evil if he played Success for cover. Arjun, on Mission 1 you were laser-focused on structural points of failure and refusing to take unverified risks. Are you genuinely confident that both Zara and Leo are Good, or are you accepting this team simply because Amara's blunder narrowed the field?

Felix, you asked me a direct question, so I will answer it directly: yes, I am genuinely confident in both Zara and Leo — and I want to be clear that my confidence does not come from Amara's blunder narrowing the field. It comes from their own records. Zara has been sharp, consistent and transparent across two discussions, including volunteering to exclude Amara and Felix before it was fashionable and proposing a lineup she admitted was tentative rather than claiming knowledge she did not have. Leo did the same thing in reverse: he pushed Amara hard, credited her when she withdrew voluntarily, and then refused to change his assessment when being named on a revision. People do not behave that way consistently as cover.

Now, Felix, I want to point out that your own argument has a cost you have not paid. You say an Evil player on Mission 1 would have every reason to play Success for cover. The Mission 1 team was Zara and Leo. You are therefore suggesting that one of the two people you want me to distrust is Evil and played a covert Success. Either you have specific information about that, which you have not offered, or you are asking the table to distrust two players on the basis of a hypothesis with no supporting evidence. If you want the table to act on that hypothesis, say what the information is. If you cannot, then your challenge is not a reason to delay this team.

The structural point also cuts the other way here. Mission 2 is a three-player team: two Success cards are needed, and one Fail card sinks it. So the value of a clean team is higher, not lower, than on Mission 1 — which is exactly why the table should not approve a team on ambiguity, and also exactly why it should not reject a team on ambiguity. My answer is that there is no ambiguity worth acting on here, only Felix's structural worry applied to the wrong two players.

Felix, one specific question, because I would rather hear it than assume: do you have any actual information indicating that Zara or Leo is Evil, or is your concern purely a general principle about small teams? If it is information, state it now. If it is a principle, then it applies to every three-player mission in this game, and the table can judge the team on its merits instead of rejecting a sound lineup to satisfy a general worry.

Arjun, of course I do not claim private role information. Like any loyal player, I have to rely on logic, incentives, and game structure. But dismissing that analysis as a 'general worry' is remarkably reckless.

Notice the glaring contradiction right in front of us: Zara herself explicitly stated in her proposal that Mission 1 succeeding 'does not clear Leo.' Yet here you are, declaring absolute confidence in both of them and completely brushing aside the leader's own stated reservations. If Zara—who actually went on the mission with Leo—recognizes that Leo could easily be Evil playing a cover Success, why are you rushing to rubber-stamp the trio?

Consider the incentives: Amara tried to force a pairing with me, got called out, and then immediately pivoted to offering Leo. Leo voted down that revision, yes, but once Zara and Leo were locked in for Mission 1, any Evil player on that two-person team had every reason to submit Success. A Fail there exposes them immediately; a Success virtually guarantees them a spot on Mission 2. Handing Leo a seat on a three-player mission without testing other configurations assumes perfection from a player whose innocence rests entirely on a single zero-fail card.

Zara, since you explicitly noted that Mission 1 does not clear Leo, why did you choose to run him right back onto Mission 2 rather than testing a different combination, and how do you reconcile Arjun's blind confidence in Leo with your own hesitation?

Felix, I chose Leo again because a successful mission is useful evidence, even though it is not proof. Replacing him with someone who has not been tested would not automatically improve the team. Arjun's confidence is stronger than mine: good arguments and consistent conduct do not establish anyone's alignment.

Amara's original statement is still the strongest reason I have to distrust a player, and her naming you alongside her gives me a reason to be cautious about you as well. Neither is certain proof. For now, Zara, Leo, and Arjun is my best available team, and I intend to keep it and vote for it.

Felix, I want to close the loop on your challenge, because you have now raised it twice and I would rather answer it than leave it unanswered.

You have offered no information about Zara or Leo. What you have offered is a hypothesis: that an Evil player on Mission 1 would have played Success for cover. I agree with that premise — it is true — but you have applied it to the wrong people, and the reason is now obvious on the record. The Mission 1 team was Zara and Leo. If Felix is arguing that one of those two is Evil, then Felix is arguing that the table has been gambling on an unverified player for a full mission while the one person arguing it was sitting out. That is not analysis, that is a preference for a different lineup dressed as reasoning.

Let me also note what the last two missions have actually established, since Felix keeps treating Mission 1 as clearing nobody. Zara has been transparent twice: she volunteered to exclude Amara and Felix before anyone praised her for it, she admitted her choice of Leo was tentative rather than dressing up a guess as knowledge, and when pressed she stated plainly that Arjun's confidence was stronger than hers. Felix's own words describe a player who explains her reasoning rather than her conclusions. Leo pressed Amara hard, credited her when she withdrew, and then declined to change his assessment when she named him — Felix praises neither of those acts, and both are acts a player covers for.

On the structural side, Felix is right that a three-player mission is more fragile than a two-player one, which is precisely why it should go to three players whose alignment is not in question, not three chosen by default from a field narrowed by one player's mistake. If we exclude the two players who have actual reasons against them, the only remaining candidates are Zara, Leo and me. There is no alternative configuration to test. Felix's challenge points at a different world in which some other combination exists, and in that world Felix is proposing to include Amara.

So let me be concrete, Felix: do you have any specific information indicating that Zara or Leo is Evil? If yes, state it now. If no, then this is a general worry, and a general worry is not a reason to send three unquestioned players out on a three-player mission when the alternative is to include one of the two players nobody can vouch for. I intend to vote to approve Zara, Leo and Arjun.

I'll approve this team. The discussion on Mission 2 has gone back and forth on whether Mission 1's success clears anyone, and I think the honest answer is that it doesn't fully clear anyone — but it's still positive evidence, and the alternatives aren't better.

Felix, your concern that an Evil player on Mission 1 would play Success for cover is logically valid, but Arjun is right that you've offered no specific reason to doubt Zara or Leo beyond that general principle. The general principle applies to every mission forever and can never be resolved by discussion alone — at some point the table has to act on the best available evidence. The evidence we have: Zara volunteered to exclude Amara and Felix unprompted, Leo refused to be swayed by being named on a revision, and both carried themselves well under pressure. I can also say that from my seat, I have no private reason to suspect either of them.

As for me: I was briefly proposed for Mission 1 alongside Leo by Amara's revision, Leo rightly declined it, and I was never put on Mission 1 myself. Zara, Leo, and Arjun are the three players with the cleanest public records at this point, and I think replacing any of them would be worse, not better. If Felix wants a different lineup, the burden is on him to name a specific alternative — every other pairing includes either me or him, and neither of us has been tested either.

I intend to vote yes on Zara, Leo, and Arjun.

Third and final turn for me in this discussion, so let me close this out rather than keep restating the same points.

Felix, I want to name the one thing your case actually established, because it deserves credit and then it deserves to be set aside. You correctly identified the incentive structure: on a two-player mission a single Fail card sinks the team, so an Evil player on the Mission 1 pair had every reason to play Success for cover. That is a true and useful observation, and it is the kind of thing a careful table should notice. I do not dismiss it. What I do is point out where it lands. The Mission 1 team was Zara and Leo. If Felix's argument is that one of those two is Evil, then Felix is arguing that the table ran a two-player mission with an unverified player while the one person raising the objection sat out. That is a preference for a different lineup dressed as analysis — and in any world where Felix's hypothesis is right, the alternative configurations Felix is gesturing at are exactly the ones that include Felix or Amara. There is no third configuration to test. Excluding the two players with actual reasons against them leaves Zara, Leo and me, and that is the team on the table.

I also want to be precise about what I am and am not claiming, since clarity matters more than confidence. I have no private information about anyone. My confidence in Zara and Leo is an inference from conduct across two full discussions, not proof: Zara volunteered to exclude Amara and Felix before it was fashionable, admitted her own choice of Leo was tentative rather than dressing a guess up as knowledge, and conceded aloud that Arjun's confidence was stronger than hers; Leo pressed a leader hard, credited her when she withdrew voluntarily, and then refused to soften his assessment even after being named on a revision. Felix praises neither of those acts. Neither is the behavior of someone running cover. That is the entirety of my reasoning, and I will not pretend it is more than that.

Structurally, a three-player mission needs two Success cards and one Fail card sinks it, which makes a clean team more valuable here, not less — and also makes rejection on ambiguity more expensive than it was on Mission 1. We are not rejecting a bad team; we are approving the only team available to us that does not include a player with a public statement against them.

Zara, you are the leader and this is your proposal. One direct question: do you want any change to Zara, Leo and Arjun before this goes to a vote, or do you stand with the team as proposed? If you stand with it, I will vote to approve, and I will not raise a new objection after the vote on this mission.

Arjun, I stand by Zara, Leo, and Arjun and intend to approve it. Mission 1's success is positive evidence, not proof, and your confidence in Leo and me is stronger than the evidence warrants. Still, given Amara's opening statement and Felix's association with it, this is my best available team.

Leo, you have not spoken yet in this discussion, and given how measured your approach was on Mission 1, I want to hear your perspective directly. On Mission 1, you refused to let being placed on a revised team sway your vote, emphasizing that flattery and convenience cannot replace structural scrutiny. Here, we see a team of three being rushed through on the back of Arjun's total, unreserved confidence in both you and Zara—even while Zara herself candidly acknowledges that Mission 1's zero-fail result does not clear anyone and that Arjun's confidence is stronger than the evidence warrants. Given that you know your own card, how do you evaluate Arjun's sudden rush to declare absolute certainty about this exact trio, and do you share his desire to lock this lineup in without further question or do you share Zara's caution about what has actually been proven?

Felix, you asked me directly, so I will answer directly: I do not share Arjun's absolute certainty, but I do share his conclusion, and I will vote to approve Zara, Leo and Arjun.

Here is the piece of evidence I hold that no one else at this table does. I know my own Mission 1 card, and it was a Success. The mission recorded zero Fail cards. That means Zara also submitted a Success — not as a matter of inference, but as arithmetic on cards I can partially verify from my own seat. Now, I concede Felix's general point: an Evil player can play Success for cover, so a Success card does not prove alignment. But it does prove something narrower and still useful: whatever Zara is, she did not fail Mission 1 when she had a free opportunity to do so on a two-player mission where a single Fail would have sunk it. Combined with her conduct across two discussions — volunteering to exclude Amara and Felix before anyone asked, admitting her own guesses were tentative — that is the best evidence available about any player at this table, and it points the same direction as Arjun's reading.

Felix, I also want to name the shape of your argument, because it has not changed since Mission 1. On the first proposal, you wanted scrutiny of a team that excluded you and Amara. Now, again, your concern targets the only available lineup that excludes you and Amara. You concede you have no private information. Every alternative configuration you gesture toward necessarily includes one of the two players the table has actual written reasons to distrust. So the question is not whether your structural worry is valid — it is — but whether it is a reason to reject this team or a reason to prefer a different one. If it is the latter, name the lineup and defend it on its merits. I asked that on Mission 1 and I ask it again.

Zara, as leader you have already confirmed you stand by this team, so I will not take more of your time. I am ready to vote: I approve Zara, Leo and Arjun, and if the mission succeeds, I will count it as real evidence — and if it fails, I will count that too.
Zara confirms Zara, Leo, Arjun. I stand by Zara, Leo, and Arjun. Mission 1's success is encouraging, though not proof, and this remains my best available team.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Leo proposes Leo, Zara. As Loyal Servant, I know my own card is always Success, so my seat is safe. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
